title: The Ṛbhus Make One Cup Four and Earn a Share
synthesis:
Almost the whole of this hymn is speech — a question, a commission, a reply, a threat, a quarrel and a joke — told from inside, with no narrator to say who is talking.

It opens in alarm. *Kim u śreṣṭhaḥ kiṃ yaviṣṭho na ājagan* — is it the eldest or the youngest who has come to us, and on what *dūtya*, what messenger's errand? Then, before any charge has been laid: *na nindima camasam*, we did not disparage the cup, which is of high family; brother {{agni}}, we spoke well of the wood. Men defending themselves against an accusation nobody has made.

The second verse states the commission, and everything hangs on it. *Ekaṃ camasaṃ caturaḥ kṛṇotana* — make the one cup into four; the gods said so, and that is why I have come, O sons of Sudhanvan. Then the wage: *sākaṃ devair yajñiyāso bhaviṣyatha*, along with the gods you shall become *yajñiya*, fit to receive sacrifice. Craftsmen are offered divinity, and the price is one impossible piece of work. They answer in the third verse by listing what such work involves — a horse to be made, a chariot, a *dhenu*, the two aged ones to be made young — and saying that having done these, brother, they will come. Nobody asks whether it can be done.

The fourth verse gives the result through someone else's eyes. The work finished, the {{ṛbhu}}s look round for the messenger, who has gone; and when {{tvaṣṭṛ}} saw the four cups made, he hid himself among the *gnās*, the divine women. The master craftsman of the gods sees the work and hides. The fifth says why: *hanāma enān*, let us kill these men who reviled the cup the gods drink from. The Ṛbhus take other names at the pressing, and by those other names the *kanyā* keeps them safe. Their escape is a change of name.

Then the sixth opens on a different scene entirely. {{indra}} has yoked his bays, the {{aśvinau}} have horsed their chariot, {{bṛhaspati}} has driven up the *viśvarūpā* cow — and the three are named for the first time, Ṛbhu, Vibhvan and Vāja, *svapasaḥ*, good workers, who went to the gods and took up *yajñiyaṃ bhāgam*, a share in the sacrifice. The promise of verse 2 is kept here, and their names arrive only once earned.

The seventh recites the works as accomplished fact — a cow drawn out of a hide *dhītibhiḥ*, by acts of thought; the aged pair made young; a horse fashioned from a horse; the chariot yoked. The instrument is {{dhī}}: this making is mental before it is manual. The eighth gives their reception at the table — drink this water, or this rinsing of the *muñja* grass, and if neither pleases you, take your pleasure at the third pressing. That is where the day's rite has kept them ever since. In the ninth they argue with no arbiter — waters are most, said one; Agni is most, said another; a third named something else to the company — and then, *ṛtā vadantaḥ camasān apiṃśata*, speaking true things, they shaped the cups. Truth-telling and good workmanship are one action here.

The tenth sets three men to butcher's work: one driving the cow down to the water, one carving the flesh laid out, one carrying off the refuse at sundown — and then the plainest line in the hymn, *kiṃ svit putrebhyaḥ pitarā upāvatuḥ*, what exactly did the parents do to help their sons? The eleventh credits them with grass on the heights and water in the hollows, *svapasyayā*, by good workmanship, and tells them not to break off today what they began. The twelfth has them creeping round the worlds with eyes shut, asking where their old parents were, cursing the man who grabbed their arm and answering back the man who spoke up. The thirteenth wakes them: Agohya, who woke us? — and the goat named the dog as the waker, and after a full year they opened their eyes on this.

The fourteenth leaves the story. The {{marut}}s travel by heaven, Agni by earth, {{vāta}} through the *antarikṣa*, {{varuṇa}} by the waters with the seas — *yuṣmān icchantaḥ*, all of them seeking you, *śavaso napātaḥ*, sons of strength. The men nearly killed over a cup are now what the moving world is looking for.
practice:
In this hymn the Ṛbhus are men. They are addressed by a patronymic — *saudhanvanāḥ*, the sons of Sudhanvan — and verse 2 puts the terms in writing: do this work and you will become *yajñiya*, entitled to a share of what is offered. Verse 6 records that they collected. Whatever else the Ṛgveda contains, it contains this: standing among the gods obtained by skilled work, on a commission, with a deadline.

The Anukramaṇī names them in fourteen sūktas. Five run consecutively in maṇḍala 4 ([[4.33]] through 4.37), and maṇḍala 1 holds four — [[1.20]], [[1.110]], [[1.111]] and this one, which is the fullest telling. Their standing hour is fixed by verse 8: the third pressing of the day, the evening savana, is theirs, and the tradition has never moved them from it.

What they are asked for is not devotion and not austerity. It is work — divide one vessel four ways without ruining it, restore youth to two worn-out people, make a cow that gives milk, build a chariot that runs. And verse 7 names the instrument: *dhītibhiḥ*, by acts of thought. The word is the *dhī* that stands behind *dhyāna*. Skill in this hymn is a form of attention, which is why verse 9 can put truth-telling and cup-making in the same breath.

Tvaṣṭṛ is the figure to notice, because he is not a villain and the hymn does not dispose of him. He is the established master of the craft. He looks at what the newcomers have made, hides himself, and then proposes killing them. Anyone who has been overtaken in their own line of work, or has overtaken someone, has met both sides of verse 4. The Ṛbhus survive it by taking other names and going on with the job.

And verse 10's question survives everything around it. Three brothers doing the whole of a hard job, and one of them asking aloud what help the parents ever were. The Ṛgveda kept the line.
disagreements:
Sāyaṇa supplies the frame the verses assume. The three Ṛbhus were at a sacrifice, about to drink soma; the gods sent Agni to see what they were doing; Agni found the three so alike that he took a like form himself — which is why they call him brother in verse 1 and cannot tell whether he is the eldest or the youngest.

Verse 4's *gnāsv antar nyānaje* is his, too: he glosses the verb *nyakto abhūt*, was made invisible, takes *gnā* as *strī* on the authority of Nirukta 3.21, and adds that Tvaṣṭṛ *striyam ātmānam amanyata* — thought himself a woman, that is, felt himself humbled. Wilson prints "he was immediately lost amongst the women"; Griffith, "concealed himself among the Consorts of the Gods."

On verse 5 Sāyaṇa makes the new names an etiology: to evade Tvaṣṭṛ the Ṛbhus took the titles *adhvaryu*, *hotā* and *udgātā*, and this, he says, is why a man officiating at a rite is always addressed by his office and never by his own name.

He also reads the sleeping Ṛbhus of verses 11–13 as the sun's rays, citing Nirukta 11.16, with *Agohya* a name of the sun — either "not to be hidden" or "not to be apprehended." On that reading verse 13's *śvan* is not a dog but *antarikṣe śvasantam vāyum*, the wind breathing in the mid-space; Wilson prints the wind, while Griffith keeps the animals: "The goat declared the hound to be your wakener."
note: ṛbhu ascriptions counted across all ten Anukramaṇī files (14 sūktas, of which 4.33-4.37 are consecutive); dhītibhiḥ verified as √dhī (dhīti) in the grammar file, not √dhā
